leading_positions.synthesis: Six of the eight round-1 files prefer B015 (Katori, Ye) as a single-part prize, and four of the six (Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) moved to it from another opening first choice. They share the case that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct, nameable idea, that Katori (concept, first strontium clock) and Ye (performance frontier near 1e-18) have separable roles, and that comparisons across laboratories and species give independent confirmation. They do not share one view of the main weakness: some stress overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes, others the unrepresented groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, Ludlow, Lemke, Lisdat) and the pending redefinition of the second. The wording of the citation (lattice concept and achieved accuracy, not combs or clocks in general) is raised in several files.

Danielsson alone prefers B014 (Halzen, Karle) as a single-part prize, as a discovery of nature in the plain sense: a diffuse TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrino flux confirmed in several IceCube channels, with source evidence (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) behind it. He states that B015 should be preferred if the committee judges clean attribution to outweigh breadth of discovery. Pearce, Eriksson, Mehlig, Lindroth and Olsson carry B014 as an alternative or rank it, but only Danielsson prefers it in the round-1 configuration. The files agree on the discovery and differ on the credit structure, the independence of confirmation and whether the source results are mature.

Eriksson alone prefers B018 (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan) as a single-part prize, citing band topology with a Z2 invariant as a new organising principle, a prediction-then-observation sequence and two decades of replication. Olsson and Mehlig keep B018 as an alternative, and Pearce carries the related B003 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue). Eriksson's own file concedes that Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers cannot fit three names and that the 2016 prize touches neighbouring ground. Whether the third name should be Hasan (B018) or Xue (B003) is not settled between the files.

areas_of_agreement: All eight files treat optical lattice clocks (B015) as scientifically mature, independently reproduced near the 1e-18 level and as having the least contested two-name credit (Katori, Ye) on the shortlist; even the two members whose first choice is another candidate (Danielsson, Eriksson) call it a serious or the safest alternative on attribution.

No file disputes that the IceCube diffuse flux (B014) and the topological-insulator programme (B018) are genuine discoveries; the disagreement is about credit and maturity, not about whether they occurred.

The files that discuss it agree that the quantum-computing candidates (B009, B039) face novelty questions from the 2012 and 2025 prizes, and that the redefinition of the second is an application milestone decided by another body, not a scientific doubt about B015, although they weigh it differently as a timing factor.
Several files agree that, if B015 is chosen, the citation should be worded around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation and not around frequency combs or optical clocks in general.
scientific_disputes: Whether the lattice clock is a distinct architecture (many-atom averaging with Lamb-Dicke confinement at the magic wavelength) or a refinement of a line already honoured by the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes (raised by Eriksson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce in their case-against statements).

Whether an instrument-driven metrological advance (B015) should rank ahead of a discovery of a new window on nature (B014) or a new class of matter (B018); Danielsson and Pearce state this as a difference of judgement, not a measurable criterion.

Whether B014 rests on the diffuse flux only, which several files accept as confirmed in multiple IceCube channels, or whether the citation can include source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane), which Danielsson, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce regard as statistically modest.

Whether B018 is a distinct recognition or an extension of the 2016 topological-phases prize (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz); Eriksson and Mehlig note that the 2016 citation did not cover the quantum spin Hall effect or three-dimensional topological insulators.

Whether fluctuation theorems (B005), preferred first at opening by Mehlig alone, have experimental reach beyond free-energy estimators and single-molecule work; Kroll, Lindroth and Eriksson ask for a decisive measurement.
attribution_disputes: B015: whether Katori (concept, first strontium lattice clock) and Ye (accuracy frontier, many-body integration) fairly cover a field with other groups and contributors (Lemonde at SYRTE, Lisdat at PTB, Ludlow, Lemke, Bloom, Hinkley, the single-ion work of Rosenband and Wineland's group); no file proposes a different set of names.

B014: whether Halzen and Karle can stand for a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors; Eriksson also names Kowalski, Klein and Waxman as outside the credit. Danielsson regards the credit as compact; Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson regard it as a real difficulty.

B018 against B003: both use Kane and Molenkamp but differ in the third name (Hasan for three-dimensional topological insulators against Xue for the quantum anomalous Hall effect); Olsson argues Xue's work is a separate achievement and that B018 is the cleaner single statement, while Eriksson and Pearce could accept either. Mele (co-author of the Kane-Mele Z2 papers) and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction) are absent from both.

Where apparently similar proposals differ: B009 and B032 both include Cirac and Zoller, which Mehlig cites as a reason for caution on B032; B039 omits Devoret, Girvin and Huang according to Kroll and Pearce, and Lindroth adds Devoret and Martinis as contested claimants.
maturity_disputes: B015: whether recognition should wait for the formal redefinition of the second. Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce say it should not; Johansson and Danielsson list it as an open question.
B014: whether independent detector confirmation (KM3NeT, Baikal-GVD still maturing) is sufficient, and whether the source population is stable enough to cite.
B018: Eriksson's and Olsson's files treat roughly two decades of replication as ample maturity; the disagreement there lies in credit, not in time.

B030 (twisted bilayer graphene, an alternative in three files): Lindroth and Kroll note that the mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated and that the experimental lead (Cao) is outside the credit.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Kroll (supporter of B015) discloses a research stay during his doctoral period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, with which Jun Ye is associated, and describes it as background rather than a personal tie; Pearce's file asks that the committee record it formally.

Johansson discloses WACQT leadership at Chalmers, succession to Per Delsing and a presentation of the 2025 prize, which may require recusal on B039 and nearby superconducting-circuit candidates; he states no specific conflict for B015. Kroll separately notes a WACQT programme-management role touching B039, B009 and B032 as a field.
Eriksson flags field proximity (electronic-structure theory) to B007 and the topological-materials candidates as a possible bias, not a recusal issue.

Pearce (the chair) notes that astroparticle work (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, balloon polarimetry) is neighbouring to B014 with no documented tie to IceCube or its named candidates, and that this closeness may have biased his earlier first-place ranking.

Lindroth notes professional familiarity with the clock community, with no documented tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names; Olsson shares Chalmers as an institution with Johansson, with no documented tie to a credited name.
questions_for_round2: For B015, should the committee treat the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes as covering the lattice clock, or can it state in a citation why the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate invention? Which wording would settle this for Eriksson, who ranked it sixth for this reason?

Can Katori and Ye be defended as the two credited names given the contributions of other groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, single-ion clocks), and does any member want to propose a different or additional name within the three-person limit?

Is the independence of the 1e-18 confirmations established by inter-laboratory comparison data across species and institutions, as Pearce and Kroll argue, or should the committee ask for that evidence directly before relying on it?

Would Danielsson, with the other members who rank B014 as an alternative, accept B015 as the prize this year, or does the committee want to resolve whether a two-name credit can fairly represent the IceCube collaboration, and whether a citation should rest on the diffuse flux alone?

Is a two-part configuration (for example B015 with B014 or B030) worth considering, given that the three-person limit forces a laureate to be dropped from one part, or should round 2 settle on a single-part prize?

If the committee wishes to consider a topological prize, should the third name be Hasan (B018) or Xue (B003), and how should Mele and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang be handled in the credit and the citation?
Should the committee record Kroll's Hall-laboratory connection and Johansson's WACQT roles formally, and does either change how the stated support for B015, B039 or other candidates is weighted?
summary.chair_observation: In the eight round-1 files, six members explicitly prefer B015 as a single-part prize, one prefers B014 and one prefers B018; every file rates B015 as the cleanest attribution, while the case against it centres on overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and on whether other groups are left out. B014 and B018 are described as broader discoveries whose credit is harder to settle. Round 2 should test the novelty and credit questions on B015 and say whether a pairing or a topological alternative offers an attribution the committee can defend.
